title: Can AI Chatbots anticipate student misconceptions?
author: Craig Barton
summary: This opens Craig Barton's three-part September 2024 series on whether AI chatbots can support teacher planning, starting with the task he considers easiest: anticipating student misconceptions. He writes his own list for subtracting negative numbers, then gives Gemini, ChatGPT, Copilot and Claude the same structured prompt asking for common errors, why students make them, an explanation and a check question. ChatGPT is judged the best, with genuinely useful explanations and checks; Claude is good and uniquely spots the misapplied two-minuses rule; Gemini and Copilot include examples that are actually correct or irrelevant. Barton concludes the output is definitely useful, given it appears in seconds against the twenty years of experience behind his own list, but warns that the bots are confident bullshitters, so teachers should sense-check and discuss the results with colleagues.
points: Anticipating misconceptions in advance lets a teacher shape the explanation and examples and plan responses before the noise of the lesson, a skill novices lack because they were successful maths students themselves.
A structured prompt asking for the example, the reason, a student-facing explanation and a check question produced richer material than a bare list of misconceptions.
ChatGPT's output rivalled or beat the author's own list, and the prompt can be reused for any topic in a scheme of work.
Several chatbot misconceptions were simply wrong, for example a correct answer offered as an error, so confident delivery is no evidence of accuracy.
Barton's recommended next step is to try the prompt on one topic, sense-check it more than once, and share the output with colleagues to discuss its effect on planning.
quotes: If teachers cannot anticipate students’ misconceptions and mistakes ahead of time, they leave themselves vulnerable to surprises in the classroom. Teachers then have to try to interpret and deal with a student's surprising wrong answer amidst the noise of a busy lesson, which rarely leads to an optimal response.
A prompt is needed to get a response from the bot, and writing a good one is quite a challenge. You need enough specificity, without being too leading.
On the surface, these look great - If you specify a response structure to a Chatbot, they are very good at complying. But when you dig a bit deeper, problems emerge.
Most impressive of all is the explanation it offers to teachers to help their students understand - I found these genuinely useful.
How long did my (inferior) list take me? Well, it took me 5 minutes to write but 20 years of experience to create. Teachers don’t have that time, and kids can’t afford to wait.
Confident bullshitters” is an apt phrase for the current state of some of these AI Chatbots, and it is easy to get suckered in.
Use my prompt or tweak it accordingly. Sense-check it more than once. Then share the output with colleagues and discuss how it could impact your planning and teaching.
